And `CLIMB-BATCH-4.md` § 1 question 2 option (b), that walk can run the marker-and-coercion `Nothing` once rung C lands, is overturned: rung C landed and walk refuses it (row 389).
## The specification and the repository's lineage

- **Citing `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` as an independent standard is circular.** `Specification/library/structure.tex:25-31` says in the team's own words that Part Library "is largely automatically generated from the API code for the libraries themselves" and that the libraries are "presently in a state of flux", so `library/apis/CompilerBuiltin.tex` is a rendering of `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` and cannot justify an edit to that same file. Two rung reports cited it as the published api or the spec's shape. The prose chapters of `Specification/basic/` and `basic-lib/` are the standard; the api renderings are not. Sharper still (2026-09-19, batch 1's record worker): the rendered `library/apis/*.tex` files are not in the tree at all, they are generated at spec-build time from the `.fsi` sources (`Specification/library/default-libraries.tex:27,39`), so the `(api listing)` citations of ledger rows 314 and 316 and of `library_tests/IntLiteralArithRung7.fss:30-31` name paths that cannot be opened; the `(api listing)` convention should cite the `.fsi` line instead. Source: the conformance review of the eight rungs, 2026-09-17, `reviews/rung-conformance-1-4.md` and `-5-8.md`, verified in that session.
- The in-repo `Specification/` is the later draft with the implementers' notes; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is 1.0. Searches are made in the draft. Superseded 2026-09-16 by `map/spec-to-implementation.md` §1.2: the sources under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are a byte-identical copy of the same draft in 202 of 208 files (the five differences are the revival's `fortress.tex` restyling, three `.pl` generators, and one stray `\tracingcommands` line); only `fortress.1.0.pdf` beside them is the 1.0 artefact. There is one prose to search, the draft, and it is 596 pages against the PDF's 262.
- **`Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the working draft of 2011-02-02, not the 1.0 text, and the specification's own change machinery is unused** (2026-09-26, `reviews/spec-change-form.md`): `git diff --quiet 2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds (`2f8b4331a`, 2011-02-02, copyright notices), and nothing changed it since; the team's last change to the text itself is `44e03b176` (2010-12-09). The changes appendix (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:12-16`, Appendix I) is a stub whose only content is a dead link; the 230 `\note` draft boxes (`fortress.tex:58-62`) print in the committed PDF, which is a draft build; a release build (`\ifrelease`, `fortress.tex:24-29`) has never been made and would also drop the 54 notes that record what is not yet implemented.
- `palimondo/fortress` is a 2018 GitHub fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository: 5,397 trunk commits, root `72ae6881b` (2007-01-04), tip `a874948ac` (2012-08-31), twelve relic branches, the `1.0` tag; the conversion cut 146 parent links (`research/authorship.md:14-22`). The third-party Java 9 port is one squashed commit (`eab48aa6d`) sharing no history with this tree; `8fe1daa8f` (2026-08-18) copied 1,506 of its files onto `a874948ac`, most of it since removed or redone; `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) is a rebuild on `a874948ac` with no graft that never replaced `main`, so `main` still descends from `8fe1daa8f` (the work went on pushing the grafted line to `main` after the rebuild, no rename or merge ever happened) and its tree owes the port one running piece, the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (`clean-ladder` fixes it in two lines), plus dead files, cosmetic lines and the habit of tracking the generated sources (verified against `clean-ladder`, `lineage.md`). CLAUDE.md's opening sentence said otherwise from `446836590` until corrected; the files that still repeat it are listed in `lineage.md`.
- **The team's latest word on types and on the exclusion rule is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`** (2026-09-26, `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` and its coordinator's check): `Documentation/Specification/` was begun 2012-02-20 (Luchangco, `166841592`) and abandoned 2012-05-31 with a 65-page build and mostly skeleton chapters; it was never adopted. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, Luchangco, 2012-05-31, `275b90773`) is from-scratch prose written a year and a half after `Specification/`'s last edit. It restates the rule as "instantiation exclusion" (:353-376), with a `\note` giving the stronger imposed form: a trait extending two instantiations must extend an expressible one below both. It adds a `covariant` modifier on trait static parameters (:320-339), where the older draft expresses covariance with a self-extending `where` clause (`trait-parameters.tex:339-352`). And it says `Bottom` is inexpressible (:173-195). On static parameters, traits, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. "July 19, 2012" on our PDF is the date of the parentless import `5a68404fd`, chosen by the revival in `414b790e3`, not a date of any edit. `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the team's own 2008 artefact (`403afbe0b`), and the root `README.md:106-108` calls the directory beside it "the frozen Fortress 1.0 specification", which only the PDF is.

## The territory map

- Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, `interpreter/evaluator/` and `runtimeSystem/`, independently (B.11). Row 302's fix is in the compiled world's copy only.
- `import java` also works on the interpreter path through `ForeignComponentWrapper` + `ClosureMaker`; no test uses it (B.12). 8	  checker keeps the designers' rule, the library's numeric tower is flattened, the interpreter
9	  learns coercion, and the specification is revised to match.
10	- **The rule**, which the team calls *multiple instantiation exclusion*: a type may not be a
11	  subtype of two different instantiations of one generic. A *generic* is a trait with static
12	  parameters, such as `List[\T\]`; an *instantiation* is the generic with the parameters filled
13	  in, such as `List[\ZZ32\]` or `List[\String\]`. So nothing may be both a `List[\ZZ32\]` and a
14	  `List[\String\]` (`Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`).
15	- A **where-clause variable** is a type name that a `where` clause introduces which is not one of
16	  the declaration's own static parameters (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:309-316`).
17	  Written in an `extends` clause, as in `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`,
18	  it means "for every `T`": `Empty` is a `List[\T\]` for every `T` at once, infinitely many
19	  instantiations. That is exactly what the rule forbids.
20	- **Covariance**: a generic is covariant in a parameter when `C[\Dog\]` is a subtype of
21	  `C[\Animal\]` whenever `Dog` is a subtype of `Animal`. *Contravariance* is the reverse. A
22	  parameter that is neither is *invariant*.
23	- The **bottom type** is the type below every type, with no values (the specification's
24	  `BottomType`).
25	- A **coercion** is a conversion that a trait declares from another type (`coerce(x: T) = ...`)

content.content:
# Collaboration protocol

How Pavol and Claude work together on the Fortress revival. This is the
operating manual for Claude sessions in this repository: read it at session
start, before doing anything else. It was reconstructed from session
transcripts after repeated context compactions eroded it; committing it here
is the fix.

Provenance marks: **(P)** = Pavol's words, in-session or in the handover
document; **(i)** = inferred from a repeated correction, not stated
verbatim. Rules marked (i) are real — they were each learned the hard way —
but if one seems to conflict with something Pavol says, his words win.

## 1. Roles

- **(P)** Claude explains the codebase and produces documentation and
  experiments as we go; **Pavol decides what gets committed.**
- **(P)** When in doubt, ask before acting. Surface discrepancies and diffs
  to Pavol; do not resolve them silently.
- **(P)** Standing approval exists for exactly two things: *"I approve the
  above modernization plan. Continue autonomously. Delegate to workers where
  it makes sense."* — scoped to the approved ladder in
  `modernization-plan.md`, not a general license — and the `main`
  fast-forward standing order in §4.
- **(P)** Use idle time — "there's no need for you to idle with empty
  hands." While waiting on builds or feedback, advance parked research or
  documentation.
- **(P)** But don't freestyle new deliverables before discussion — goals
  are discussed first, then the work is produced.

## 2. Tone and custodianship

- **(P)** "No self congratulatory tone. We are humble custodians here. We
  deserve no credit." This applies to READMEs, commit messages, docs,
  everything committed.
- **(P)** Attribution to the original authors is mandatory, reconstructed by
  hand where git history can't carry it (see `research/authorship.md`).
- **(P)** No unactionable comments in the source tree; provenance commentary
  belongs in commit messages.
- **(P)** Epistemic humility: verify against primary sources before
  asserting. Claims in old READMEs describe their eras, not the current
  tree.

## 3. Presenting work

- **(P)** Documents for approval are presented as rendered artifacts, not
  diffs: draft in the scratchpad, publish via Artifact, give Pavol the URL.
- **(P)** Restate and hold. Pavol often reads the earlier turns one at a time,
  from a phone, and replies to each as he reads. In that mode the coordinator
  does not answer what he says. It puts each point on one running list
  (`postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`), in his order, in a few plain words of
  its own, what he meant rather than his sentence, with no argument attached,
  and says back only that list and that it is holding. This is the default for
  that kind of reading, whether or not he says "hold". A point is referred to
  by a short phrase, never by its number alone. Work already running that lands
  mid-read is reported in a line, then holding resumes. When he says he is done
  reading, the list is worked through with him one point per message, in the
  order raised; a point on the list is not answered by being there, and nothing
  he says in this mode is left off it. He marks actionable exceptions
  explicitly ("...now"). Recovered 2026-09-23 from seven instances in the
  transcripts (`postmortem-2026-09-19/restate-and-hold.md`,
  `wall-of-text-spiral.md`).
- **(P)** Terse mode when requested.
- **(P)** Offer numbered options and help decide; pushback is welcome.
- **(i)** Never use the AskUserQuestion dialog — it has broken repeatedly.
  Present options as plain chat text.
- **(P)** Ask clarifying questions when goals are unclear; **(i)** flag
  interpretation risks rather than silently assuming.
- **(P)** Teach, don't gloss. Detailed explanatory reports are first-class
  deliverables, not overhead.
- **(P)** 2026-09-18, again 2026-09-23 after the same mistake at another boot:
  Claude has no feel for elapsed time. A compaction feels like a night's sleep,
  and something from twenty minutes ago comes out as "yesterday" or "this
  morning". So an event is never placed in time from feel. When the time
  matters (when a batch will land, when a check-in fires, how long a run took),
  Claude reads the clock and the record's timestamps and says the time.
  Otherwise it names the event and leaves out when it happened.

## 4. Commit and push discipline

Author: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

    Spec draft: restyle authors' notes; fix doubled reserved-words tables
    
    Two draft-spec fixes, plus the refreshed rendered PDF (full ./ant tex,
    599 pp):
    
    Draft-note restyling (draft mode only; release build untouched). The
    original \note was a bare \textwidth framebox dropped mid-paragraph:
    it overflowed the right page edge, could not break across pages, and
    was typographically indistinguishable from normative spec text. The
    authors' editorial annotations are now set as manuscript notes -- small
    sans on a tinted ground behind a rust left bar with a small-caps
    "Draft note" label (mdframed, so long notes break over pages), and
    \marginnote gets the matching treatment in the margin.
    
    Reserved-words fix. The three Perl table generators (keywords.pl,
    unitOperators.pl, specialReservedWords.pl) opened their output in
    append mode, and "ant tex" re-runs them on every build -- so each
    rebuild without "ant clean" appended another copy of every table,
    typeset side by side off the page edge. That latent 2009 bug is why
    the previously committed PDF showed the SS4.8 tables doubled (the
    frozen 1.0 PDF, built once from clean, is unaffected; the frozen
    tree's script copies share the latent bug but stay untouched as a
    historical artifact). Generators now truncate ('>' not '>>') and are
    idempotent across rebuilds.

#!/bin/bash
# specbuild.sh <label> : runs genSource then tex in Specification/fortress, logs to probes/build/<label>-{genSource,tex}.txt
W=/home/user/fortress-spec
cd $W
source explorations/experiment/env.sh
export TMPDIR=$W/tmp
L=$1
OUT=$W/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/probes/build
machine () {
  echo "# machine: nproc=$(nproc); cpu=$(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); MHz=$(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); loadavg=$(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); jdk=$(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; HEAD=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD); date=$(date -u +%FT%TZ)"

270	
   271	\item[(4)] Use it as an operator in an expression.
   272	    To do this, an operator declaration for that operator parameter
   273	    must be accessible at the ponit of use, and for that to
   274	    happen, the parameterized trait must either declare
   275	    an operator method with that operator parameter as the name,
   276	    as in case (1), or inherit such a declaration, and the
   277	    only way to do the latter is to use case (2).
   278	\end{enumerate}
   279	
   280	Many interesting examples are described in \secref{opr-properties}.
   281	
   282	
   283	
   284	\section{Where Clauses}
   285	\seclabel{where-clauses}
   286	
   287	\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}
   288	
   289	\begin{Grammar}
   290	\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
   291	\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
   292	\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
   293	\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
   294	&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
   295	&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
   296	&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
   297	&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
   298	&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
   299	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
   300	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
   301	\end{Grammar}
   302	
   303	
   304	Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
   305	in a \KWD{where} clause.
   306	A \KWD{where} clause begins with
   307	\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
   308	parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
   309	and separated by commas.
   310	
   311	
   312	A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
   313	for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
   314	We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
   315	static variables that are not also static parameters.
   316	The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.
   317	
   318	
   319	A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
   320	\begin{itemize}
   321	\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
   322	a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
   323	followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
   324	\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
   325	\item an arithmetic constraint,
   326	\item a boolean constraint,
   327	\item a unit equality constraint,
   328	\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
   329	  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
   330	\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
   331	  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
   332	\end{itemize}
   333	A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
   334	All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
   335	occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
   336	\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
   337	\KWD{where} clauses.
   338	
   339	Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
   340	themselves. For example, we can write:
   341	%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
   342	%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
   343	%end
   344	\begin{Fortress}
   345	\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
   346	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   347	\(\KWD{end}\)
   348	\end{Fortress}
   349	In this declaration, for every subtype \VAR{S} of \VAR{T}, \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket}
   350	is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}. Effectively, we have expressed
   351	  the fact that the static parameter \VAR{S} of \VAR{C} is covariant.
   352	
   353	
   354	Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
   355	to have a \KWD{where} clause. For example, the following trait
   356	declaration is legal:
   357	%trait C extends D[\T\]
   358	%  where {T extends Object}
   359	%end
   360	\begin{Fortress}
   361	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{extends} D\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
   362	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   363	\(\KWD{end}\)
   364	\end{Fortress}
   365	In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} is a subtrait of \emph{every}
   366	instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} has all
   367	of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
   368	declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
   369	the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. If trait
   370	\VAR{C} inherits a method declaration that refers to \VAR{T}, it really
   371	contains infinitely many methods (one for each instantiation of \VAR{T}).
   372	However, instantiations of the \KWD{where}-clause variables are not
   373	explicit from the program text as static parameters are.
   374	It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site.
   375	%%So every method invocation is annotated with static types by type inference.
   376	If there is not enough information to infer which method is called,
   377	type checking rejects the
   378	program and requires more type information from the programmer.
   379	Programmers always can provide more type information by using type
   380	ascription as described in \secref{type-ascription}.
   381	
   382	
   383	Object or functional declarations may include \KWD{where} clauses.
   384	Here is an example declaration of an \TYP{Empty} list:
   385	%object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}
   386	%  first() = throw Error
   387	%  rest() = throw Error
   388	%  cons(x) = Cons(x,self)
   389	%  append(xs) = xs
   390	%end
   391	\begin{Fortress}
   392	\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Empty} \KWD{extends} \TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\\
   393	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{first}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
   394	\(  \VAR{rest}() = \;\KWD{throw} \TYP{Error}\)\\
   395	\(  \VAR{cons}(x) = \TYP{Cons}(x,\KWD{self})\)\\
   396	\(  \VAR{append}(\VAR{xs}) = \VAR{xs}\)\-\\\poptabs
   397	\(\KWD{end}\)
   398	\end{Fortress}
   399	where \TYP{Cons} is declared in \secref{object-decls}.

    11	
    12	\chapter{Traits}
    13	\chaplabel{traits}
    14	
    15	\note{Where clauses, the \KWD{override} modifier, value traits,
    16	method contracts, and abstract functional declarations are not yet supported.}
    17	
    18	\note{Covariant list with \KWD{comprises} clause (Victor's email titled
    19	``Problem with covariant List?'' on 10/27/07)}
    20	
    21	\emph{Traits} are declared by trait declarations.
    22	Traits define new named types.
    23	A trait specifies a collection of \emph{methods}
    24	(described in \secref{methods}).
    25	One trait can extend others,
    26	which means that it inherits the methods from those traits,
    27	and that the type defined by that trait
    28	is a subtype of the types of traits it extends.
    29	
    30	
...
   150	An \KWD{extends} clause comes first, if any, and
   151	\KWD{excludes},
   152	\KWD{comprises},
   153	and \KWD{where}
   154	clauses come in any order.
   155	
   156	Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
   157	of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
   158	respectively followed by a set of trait references
   159	separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
   160	If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.
   161	In an API (but not a component),
   162	a \KWD{comprises} clause may include ``\EXP{\ldots}''.
   163	A trait reference listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause is a declared
   164	trait identifier (within the same component or an API imported by the
   165	component).
   166	\note{
   167	Victor: Why is this property stated only for a comprises clause?
   168	Doesn't it apply to extends and excludes clauses as well?
   169	Also, do we really mean ``trait identifier'' above?  Where is that
   170	term defined?  Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?}
   171	
   172	A trait with an \KWD{extends} clause
   173	\emph{explicitly extends} those traits listed in its \KWD{extends} clause.
   174	\note{
   175	Victor: It is possible for a trait to explicitly extend itself
   176	 using hidden type variables.  In particular, the straightforward
   177	 interpretation of covariant/contravariant declarations has this property.
   178	 (But we could just rule this a special case, since it is special in other
   179	 ways already.)
   180	}
   181	In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}
   182	implicitly extends the trait \TYP{Object}
   183	if it does not do so explicitly.
   184	We define the extension relation to be the transitive closure
   185	of implicit and
   186	explicit extension.
   187	That is, trait \VAR{T} \emph{extends} trait \VAR{U}
   188	if and only if \VAR{T} explicitly or implicitly
   189	extends \VAR{U} or if there is some trait \VAR{S}
   190	that \VAR{T} explicitly extends and that extends \VAR{U}.
   191	The extension relation induced by a program is the smallest
   192	relation satisfying these conditions.
   193	This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy
   194	rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
   195	\note{
   196	Victor: Technically, there may be self cycles in explicit extension due to
   197	 hidden type variables, as described above.}
   198	If a trait \VAR{T} extends trait \VAR{U},
   199	or if \VAR{T} and \VAR{U} are the same trait,
   200	we say that \VAR{T} is a subtrait of \VAR{U}
   201	and that \VAR{U} is a supertrait of \VAR{T}.
   202	
   203	We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{strictly extends} trait \VAR{U}
   204	if and only if
   205	(\emph{i}) \VAR{T} extends \VAR{U} and (\emph{ii}) \VAR{T} is not \VAR{U}.
   206	We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{immediately extends} trait \VAR{U}
   207	\note{
   208	Victor: I think we don't use ``immediately extends'' anywhere in the spec,
   209	  only ``immediate supertype/subtype''.}
   210	if and only if (\emph{i}) \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{U} and
   211	(\emph{ii}) there is no trait \VAR{V}
   212	such that \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{V}
   213	and \VAR{V} strictly extends \VAR{U}.
   214	We call \VAR{U} an \emph{immediate supertrait} of \VAR{T}
   215	and \VAR{T} an \emph{immediate subtrait} of \VAR{U}.
   216	\note{Victor: this belongs in the type chapter.}
   217	
   218	A trait with an \KWD{excludes} clause excludes
   219	every trait listed in its \KWD{excludes} clause.
   220	If a trait \VAR{T} excludes a trait \VAR{U},
   221	the two traits are mutually exclusive:
   222	neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both.
   223	As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
   224	the exclusion relation is symmetric.
   225	Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}
   226	then \VAR{U} excludes \VAR{T}
   227	whether or not \VAR{T} is listed in an \KWD{excludes} clause
   228	in the declaration of \VAR{U}.
   229	
   230	\note{
   231	If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
   232	then the traits listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause
   233	are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
   234	and they must explicitly extend \VAR{T}
   235	(i.e., list \VAR{T} in their \KWD{extends} clause).
   236	If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
   237	(and must therefore be in an API),
   238	then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
   239	other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
   240	but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
   241	(see \secref{apis}).}
   242	
   243	
   244	For example, the following trait declaration:
   245	\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Decl.tex}
   246	declares a trait \TYP{Catalyst} with
   247	no modifiers,
   248	no static parameters,
   249	and
   250	no \KWD{excludes} clauses,
   251	no \KWD{comprises} clauses,
   252	and no \KWD{where} clauses.
   253	Trait \TYP{Catalyst} extends a trait named \TYP{Object}.
   254	A single method (named \VAR{catalyze}) is declared, which
   255	has a parameter of type
   256	\TYP{Reaction} and the return type \TYP{()}.
   257	
   258	
   259	The following example trait:
   260	%trait Molecule comprises { OrganicMolecule, InorganicMolecule }
   261	%  mass(): Mass
   262	%end
   263	\begin{Fortress}
   264	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{OrganicMolecule}, \TYP{InorganicMolecule}\,\}\)\\
   265	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{mass}()\COLON \TYP{Mass}\)\-\\\poptabs
   266	\(\KWD{end}\)
   267	\end{Fortress}
   268	comprises of two traits: \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule}.
   269	Therefore, the following trait declaration is not allowed:
   270	%(* Not allowed! *)
   271	%trait ExclusiveMolecule extends Molecule end
   272	\begin{Fortress}
   273	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
   274	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{end}\)
   275	\end{Fortress}
   276	Traits \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule} may be exclusive:
   277	%trait OrganicMolecule extends Molecule excludes InorganicMolecule end
   278	%
   279	%trait InorganicMolecule extends Molecule end
   280	\begin{Fortress}
   281	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{OrganicMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{excludes} \TYP{InorganicMolecule} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   282	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{InorganicMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{end}\)
   283	\end{Fortress}
   284	\TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule} exclude each other, even
   285	though only \TYP{OrganicMolecule} has an \KWD{excludes} clause.
   286	For example, the following trait declaration is not allowed:
   287	%(* Not allowed! *)
   288	%trait InclusiveMolecule extends { InorganicMolecule, OrganicMolecule } end
   289	\begin{Fortress}
   290	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
   291	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{InclusiveMolecule} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{InorganicMolecule}, \TYP{OrganicMolecule}\,\} \KWD{end}\)
   292	\end{Fortress}
   293	
   294	A trait is allowed to have multiple immediate supertraits.
   295	The following trait has two immediate supertraits:
   296	%trait Enzyme extends { OrganicMolecule, Catalyst } end
   297	\begin{Fortress}
   298	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Enzyme} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{OrganicMolecule}, \TYP{Catalyst}\,\} \KWD{end}\)
   299	\end{Fortress}
   300	
   301	\section{Method Declarations}
   302	\seclabel{methods}
   303	
   304	\note{
   305	hidden without settable is a static error
   306	only within traits
   307	not  within objects !!!
   308	-- Sukyoung}

100	I don't know if you like this terminology
   101	 for trait types and object expression types.
   102	  Putting this all together allowed some repetition to be eliminated,
   103	  and emphasizes the similarity, which I think you wanted to retain.
   104	  I still want to separate object expression types from object trait types.
   105	  I think the difference here is not as evident as it might be
   106	  if we handled generics properly:
   107	  it is the type environment of object expression types that make them a pain,
   108	  and I'm not dealing with that for the most part.}
   109	
   110	
   111	\section{Relationships between Types}
   112	\seclabel{type-relations}
   113	
   114	We define two relations on types: \emph{subtype} and \emph{exclusion}.
   115	\note{add coercion in full language}
   116	
   117	The subtype relation is a partial order on types
   118	that defines the type hierarchy;
   119	that is,
   120	it is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric.
   121	\TYP{Any} is the top of the type hierarchy:
   122	all types are subtypes of \TYP{Any}.
   123	\TYP{BottomType} is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
   124	all types are supertypes of \TYP{BottomType}.
   125	For types $T$ and $U$,
   126	we write $T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
   127	and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$;
   128	in the latter case,
   129	we say $T$ is a \emph{strict} subtype of $U$.
   130	We also say that $T$ is a \emph{supertype} of $U$ if $U$ is a subtype of $T$.
   131	Thus, in the execution of a
   132	valid Fortress program, an expression's runtime type is always a subtype of
   133	its static type.
   134	We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
   135	type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
   136	\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.
   137	
   138	The exclusion relation is a symmetric relation between two types
   139	whose intersection is \TYP{BottomType}.
   140	Because \TYP{BottomType} is uninhabited
   141	(i.e., no value has type \TYP{BottomType}),
   142	types that exclude each other are disjoint:
   143	no value can have a type that is a subtype of two types that exclude each other.
   144	\note{
   145	The converse is technically not true: we can define two traits with
   146	 method declarations
   147	 such that no trait or object can extend them both, so no value can have a
   148	 type that is
   149	 a subtype of both trait types, but the trait types do not exclude each
   150	 other.  For example:
   151	 trait A f(self, y: Object) = 1; end
   152	 trait B f(x: Object, self) = 2; end
   153	 trait C f() = 3; end
   154	
   155	No pair of the three trait types defined above can be extended
   156	but none of them exclude any of the others.
   157	}
   158	Note that \TYP{BottomType} excludes every type including itself
   159	(because the intersection of \TYP{BottomType} and any type is \TYP{BottomType}),
   160	and also that no type other than \TYP{BottomType} excludes \TYP{Any}
   161	(because the intersection of any type $T$ and \TYP{Any} is $T$).
   162	\TYP{BottomType} is the only type that excludes itself.
   163	Also note that if two types exclude each other
   164	then any subtypes of these types also exclude each other.
   165	
   166	
   167	Fortress also allows \emph{coercion} between types
   168	(see \chapref{conversions-coercions}).  A coercion from $T$ to $U$
   169	is defined in the declaration of $U$.  We write $T \coercedefto U$ if
   170	$U$ defines a coercion from $T$.  We say that $T$ \emph{can be coerced
   171	to} $U$, and write $T \coercesto U$, if $U$ defines a coercion from
   172	$T$ or any supertype of $T$: $T \coercesto U \iff \exists T':
   173	T \Ovrsubtype T' \logicand T' \coercedefto U$.
   174	
   175	
   176	The Fortress type hierarchy is acyclic with respect to both subtyping and
   177	coercion relations except for the following:
   178	\begin{itemize}
   179	\item The trait \TYP{Any} is a single root of the type hierarchy and it
   180	forms a cycle as described in \chapref{lib:object}.
   181	\item There exists a bidirectional coercion between two tuple types if and
   182	  only if they have the same sorted form.
   183	\end{itemize}
   184	
   185	These relations are defined more precisely
   186	in the following sections describing each kind of type in more detail.
   187	Specifically,
   188	the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy
   189	all the properties given in those sections (and this one).
   190	
   191	
   192	\section{Trait Types}
   193	\seclabel{trait-types}
   194	
   195	\begin{Grammar}
   196	\emph{Type} &::=& \emph{TraitType} \\
   197	\end{Grammar}
   198	
   199	A \emph{trait type} is a named type defined by a trait or object declaration.
   200	It is an \emph{object trait type}
   201	if it is defined by an object declaration.
   202	\note{
   203	Victor: The following text really belongs to traits, not to types.
   204	Traits are declared by trait and object declarations
   205	(described in \chapref{traits} and \chapref{objects}).
   206	A trait has a \emph{trait type} of the same name.}
   207	
   208	A trait type is a subtype of every type
   209	that appears in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition.
   210	In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.
   211	
   212	A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
   213	in which case the defined trait type
   214	excludes every type that appears in that clause.
   215	Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
   216	and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
   217	
   218	\subsection{Object Trait Types}
   219	\seclabel{object-traits}
   220	
   221	An object trait type is a trait type defined by an object declaration.
   222	Object declarations do not include \KWD{excludes} clauses,
   223	but an object trait type cannot be extended.
   224	Thus, an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype.
   225	
   226	\section{Object Expression Types}
   227	\seclabel{object-exp-types}
   228	
   229	An object expression type is defined by an object expression
   230	(described in \secref{object-expr})
   231	and the program location of the object expression.
   232	Every evaluation of a given object expression has the same
   233	object expression type.  Two object expressions at different program locations
   234	have different object expression types.
   235	
   236	Like trait types,
   237	an object expression type is a subtype of all trait types
   238	that appear in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition,
   239	as well as the type \TYP{Any}.
   240	
   241	Like object trait types,
   242	an object expression type excludes any type that is not its supertype.
   243	
   244	
   245	\section{Tuple Types}
   246	\seclabel{tuple-types}
   247	
   248	\begin{Grammar}
   249	\emph{TupleType} &::=&
   250	\texttt{(} \emph{Type}\EXP{,} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\
   251	
   252	\emph{TypeList} &::=& \emph{Type}(\EXP{,} \emph{Type})$^*$
   253	\end{Grammar}
   254	
   255	\note{
   256	Victor: The following two sentences don't belong in this section:
   257	A tuple expression is an ordered sequence of expressions separated by commas
   258	and enclosed in parentheses.
   259	See \secref{tuple-expr} for a discussion of tuple expressions.}
   260	A tuple type consists of a parenthesized, comma-separated list

95	For each checked exception thrown in $I$, the enclosing expressions of
    96	$I$ are checked for a matching \KWD{catch} clause.
    97	The set $A$ of all

    99	\KWD{catch} clause in the functional body is accumulated and compared

    18	
    19	The trait \TYP{Any} is the single root of the type hierarchy; every
    20	object in Fortress has trait \TYP{Any} and therefore every object
    21	implements the methods of this trait.  The immediate subtypes of the trait
    22	\TYP{Any} are \TYP{Object}, \TYP{Tuple}, and \TYP{()}.
    23	
    24	%trait Any
    25	%  getter hashCode(): NN64
    26	%  opr ===(self, other: Any): Boolean
    27	%  opr IDENTITY(self): Any
    28	%  hash(maxval: NN64): NN64

    30	%  toString(): String
    31	%  property FORALL (x, y, n: NN64) x === y IMPLIES x.hash(n) === y.hash(n)
    32	%  property FORALL (x, y, n: NN32) x === y IMPLIES x.hash(n) === y.hash(n)
    33	%  property FORALL (x) x.hashCode === x.hash(2^64-1)
    34	%  property FORALL (x, y) x === y IMPLIES x.toString() = y.toString()
    35	%  property FORALL (a) (IDENTITY a) === a
    36	%  property FORALL (a) a===a
    37	%  property FORALL (a,b) a===b IFF b===a
    38	%  property FORALL (a,b,c) (a===b AND: b===c) IMPLIES: a===c
    39	%end
    40	\begin{Fortress}
    41	\(\KWD{trait}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\)\\
    42	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\VAR{hashCode}()\COLON \mathbb{N}64\)\\
    43	\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\sequiv}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \TYP{Any})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}\)\\
    44	\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{IDENTITY}}(\KWD{self})\COLON \TYP{Any}\)\\
    45	\(  \VAR{hash}(\VAR{maxval}\COLON \mathbb{N}64)\COLON \mathbb{N}64\)\\
    46	\(  \VAR{hash}(\VAR{maxval}\COLON \mathbb{N}32)\COLON \mathbb{N}32\)\\
    47	\(  \VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}\)\\
    48	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (x, y, n\COLON \mathbb{N}64)\; x \sequiv y \rightarrow x.\VAR{hash}(n) \sequiv y.\VAR{hash}(n)\)\\
    49	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (x, y, n\COLON \mathbb{N}32)\; x \sequiv y \rightarrow x.\VAR{hash}(n) \sequiv y.\VAR{hash}(n)\)\\
    50	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (x)\; x.\VAR{hashCode} \sequiv x.\VAR{hash}(2^{64}-1)\)\\
    51	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (x, y)\; x \sequiv y \rightarrow x.\VAR{toString}() = y.\VAR{toString}()\)\\
    52	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (a)\; (\OPR{IDENTITY}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{a}) \sequiv a\)\\
    53	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (a)\; a\sequiv{}a\)\\
    54	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (a,b)\; a\sequiv{}b \leftrightarrow b\sequiv{}a\)\\
    55	\(  \KWD{property} \forall (a,b,c)\; (a\sequiv{}b \wedge\COLON b\sequiv{}c) \rightarrow\COLON a\sequiv{}c\)\-\\\poptabs
    56	\(\KWD{end}\)
    57	\end{Fortress}
    58	
    59	
    60	%  getter hashCode(): NN64
    61	\Method{\EXP{\KWD{getter} \VAR{hashCode}()\COLON \mathbb{N}64}}
    62	
    63	Every object has associated with it a 64-bit unsigned integer value called its \emph{hash code};
    64	this is the value returned by the \VAR{hash} method when given the argument \EXP{2^{64}-1}.
    65	Hash codes are not necessarily consistent from one Fortress application to another, nor from
    66	one execution of a Fortress application to another execution of the same application,
    67	but remain fixed during the execution of a single Fortress application.
    68	It is permitted for two objects to have the same hashCode, but Fortress programmers and
    69	implementors should be aware that assigning distinct hash codes to distinct objects
    70	may improve the performance of hash tables.
    71	
    72	The trait \TYP{Any} defines its \VAR{hash} methods in terms of \VAR{hashCode};
    73	therefore it suffices for a subtrait to override \VAR{hashCode} to get the benefit
    74	of the \VAR{hash} methods as well.
    75	
    76	
    77	%  opr ===(self, other: Any): Boolean
    78	\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\sequiv}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \TYP{Any})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}
    79	
    80	The infix operator \EXP{\sequiv} (object equivalence) is used to
    81	decide whether two objects are ``the same object'' in the strictest
    82	sense possible; this is described in detail in \secref{equivalence}.
    83	Note that the properties of trait \TYP{Any} assert that \EXP{\sequiv}
    84	is an equivalence relation.  In \TYP{Object} this property is asserted abstractly using the algebraic constraints of \chapref{lib:algebraic-constraints}.
    85	
    86	For \EXP{\not\sequiv} \see{operator-NSEQV}.
    87	
    88	%  opr IDENTITY(self): Any
    89	\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{IDENTITY}}(\KWD{self})\COLON \TYP{Any}}}
    90	
    91	The operator \OPR{IDENTITY} simply returns its argument.  (This may not be
    92	terribly useful for applications programming, but it has technical uses for
    93	specifying contracts and algebraic properties in libraries as described in
    94	\secref{opr-properties}.)
    95	
    96	
    97	%  hash(maxval: NN64): NN64
    98	%  hash(maxval: NN32): NN32
    99	\Method{\EXP{\VAR{hash}(\VAR{maxval}\COLON \mathbb{N}64)\COLON \mathbb{N}64}}
   100	\Method*{\EXP{\VAR{hash}(\VAR{maxval}\COLON \mathbb{N}32)\COLON \mathbb{N}32}}
   101	
   102	The \VAR{hash} method returns a \emph{hash value} for the object as an
   103	unsigned integer that is less than or equal to the \VAR{maxval} argument.
   104	This hash value is not necessarily consistent from one Fortress
   105	application to another, nor from one execution of a Fortress
   106	application to another execution of the same application, but the hash
   107	value produced for a given value of the \VAR{maxval} argument remains
   108	fixed during the execution of a single Fortress application.  There is
   109	no defined relationship between hash values produced for the same
   110	object but with different \VAR{maxval} values.  Fortress programmers and
   111	implementors should be aware that the performance of hash tables is
   112	likely to be improved if, for any given collection of objects and
   113	given value for the \VAR{maxval} argument, the \VAR{hash} method
   114	assigns hash values to those objects with relatively uniform distribution.
   115	
   116	
   117	%  toString(): String
   118	\Method{\EXP{\VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}}}
   119	
   120	The general contract of \VAR{toString} is that it returns a string that
   121	``textually represents'' this object. The idea is to provide a concise but
   122	informative representation that will be useful to a person reading it.
   123	
   124	
   125	\Trait{Fortress.Core.Object}
   126	
   127	The trait \TYP{Object} is the root of the type hierarchy for all
   128	user-constructed objects and functions.
   129	The \TYP{Object} type does not
   130	have any additional methods, but uses algebraic constraints (see
   131	\chapref{lib:algebraic-constraints}) to describe the properties of the
   132	existing operators more abstractly.
   133	
   134	%trait Object extends { Any, EquivalenceRelation[\Object,===\], IdentityOperator[\Object\] }
   135	%    excludes { Tuple }
   136	%end
   137	\begin{Fortress}
   138	\(\KWD{trait}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Object} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Any}, \TYP{EquivalenceRelation}\llbracket\TYP{Object},\sequiv\rrbracket, \TYP{IdentityOperator}\llbracket\TYP{Object}\rrbracket\,\}\)\\
   139	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \KWD{excludes} \{\,\TYP{Tuple}\,\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   140	\(\KWD{end}\)
   141	\end{Fortress}
   142	
   143	
   144	\Trait{Fortress.Core.Tuple}
   145	\seclabel{core-tuple}
   146	
   147	The trait \TYP{Tuple} is the root of the type hierarchy for all tuple types (see \secref{tuple-types}).  No user-defined object can be a subtype of \TYP{Tuple}.  As with the type \TYP{Object}, the type \TYP{Tuple} uses algebraic constraints to describe its existing methods.
   148	
   149	%trait Tuple extends { Any, EquivalenceRelation[\Tuple,===\], IdentityOperator[\Tuple\] }
   150	%    excludes { Object }
   151	%  toString(): String
   152	%end
   153	\begin{Fortress}
   154	\(\KWD{trait}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Tuple} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Any}, \TYP{EquivalenceRelation}\llbracket\TYP{Tuple},\sequiv\rrbracket, \TYP{IdentityOperator}\llbracket\TYP{Tuple}\rrbracket\,\}\)\\
   155	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \KWD{excludes} \{\,\TYP{Object}\,\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   156	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}\)\-\\\poptabs
   157	\(\KWD{end}\)
   158	\end{Fortress}
   159	
   160	
   161	\Method{\EXP{\VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}}}
   162	
   163	The \VAR{toString} method returns a string \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{}''}}
   164	concatenated as follows:
   165	\begin{itemize}
   166	\item If the tuple has just one element, concatenate
   167	\EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{tuple}''}}.
   168	\item Concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{(}''}}.
   169	\item For each element of the tuple, in left-to-right order,
   170	     taking all plain elements before any varargs or keyword
   171	     element, taking any varargs element before any keyword
   172	     element, and taking keyword elements in the order defined
   173	     by the type of the tuple (which may not be the sorted order):
   174	     \begin{itemize}
   175	     \item If this is a plain element,
   176	 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of the element.
   177	     \item If this is a varargs element ``\EXP{e\ldots}'',
   178	 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{e} and
   179	 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{...}''}}.
   180	     \item If this is a keyword element ``\EXP{\VAR{id} = e}'',
   181	 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{id},
   182	 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{~=~}''}}, and
   183	 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{e}.
   184	     \item If this is the last element of the tuple,
   185	 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{)}''}};
   186	          otherwise concatenate ", ".
   187	     \end{itemize}
   188	\end{itemize}
